newsitem.title: ITALY: Generals hit back in Italian troops scandal.
newsitem.headline: Generals hit back in Italian troops scandal.

text.p: Italian army generals hit back on Tuesday at allegations that troops in Somalia engaged in killings, torture and rape, saying many of the accusations were false or exaggerated.

"I believe that the affair has been blown up by the newspapers," General Gianfranco Vannucchi, head of an internal armed forces investigation into the behaviour of the troops, was quoted by newspapers as saying.
"I am confident that the whole truth will emerge. That is what we are working towards," he said.

The allegations, based on photographs and interviews with Italian soldiers who served in Somalia as part of a multinational United Nations force from late 1992 to early 1994, have been published over the past two weeks in the news magazine Panorama.

They have caused a scandal in Italy and prompted the government last Friday to set up its own inquiry after Panorama carried photos of what appeared to be the sexual assault of a young Somali woman by soldiers using a military flare.
The magazine also quoted a former soldier, Benedetto Bertini, as saying that fellow troops used Somali civilians for "target practice".
The two commanding officers of the Italian force in Somalia, General Bruno Loi and General Carmine Fiore, resigned last Saturday.
Fiore was quoted on Tuesday as saying the allegations of gratuitous killings of Somali civilians were "ridiculous and invented".
"The truth is that money has been flying around," he told Corriere della Sera newspaper, alleging that large sums had changed hands for the Panorama photographs, taken by soldiers.
He said he was confident that "I and my men will emerge from this dirty affair with our heads held high".
Panorama defended its work on Tuesday, with editor Giuliano Ferrara saying the military was trying to play down the scandal.
The allegations have caused deep shock in Italy, a former colonial power in Somalia which has taken pride in the role of its military in peacekeeping efforts abroad.
They also coincide with Italian leadership of a multinational security force deployed in Albania, where elections are due to be held on June 29.
Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta told parliament that the government-appointed commission would brook "no hesitation, no cover-ups and no delay" to get to the truth.
But he too called for a sense of proportion in the scandal, saying the armed forces as a whole should not be demonised.

"We owe the truth to the Somali people and also to the armed forces which run the risk of being collectively accused and stained before there has even been time to make the necessary investigations," Andreatta said.
